questions.knowledgeNote: Angles 1:2:3 of 180 deg are 30/60/90: sides go as sin30:sin60:sin90 = 1:sqrt(3):2.
questions.question: AQ7(i). If the angles of a triangle are to one another as 1:2:3, prove that the corresponding sides are 1:sqrt(3):2.
questions.solution: Let the angles be k, 2k, 3k with k + 2k + 3k = 180 deg, so k = 30 deg: angles 30, 60, 90 deg. By the sine rule a:b:c = sin30:sin60:sin90 = (1/2):(sqrt(3)/2):1 = 1:sqrt(3):2.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q7(i); book p189 = PDF p216 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Smallest side sqrt(13) is opposite the smallest angle: cosine rule gives cos = sqrt(3)/2.
questions.question: AQ7(ii). If the sides of a triangle are 7 cms, 4*sqrt(3) cms, sqrt(13) cms, prove that the smallest angle is 30 deg.
questions.solution: The smallest angle is opposite the smallest side sqrt(13). By the cosine rule, cos = [7^2 + (4*sqrt(3))^2 - (sqrt(13))^2]/[2*7*4*sqrt(3)] = (49 + 48 - 13)/(56*sqrt(3)) = 84/(56*sqrt(3)) = 3/(2*sqrt(3)) = sqrt(3)/2. Hence the smallest angle is 30 deg.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q7(ii); book p189 = PDF p216 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Angles in A.P. force the middle to 60 deg; then b:c = sinB:sinC pins C = 45 deg.
questions.question: AQ7(iii). The angles of a triangle ABC are in A.P., and it is given that b:c = sqrt(3):sqrt(2). Find angle A. (Printed Answers line reads '7.(ii) 75 deg' - a label slip for 7.(iii); 7.(ii) is a proof with no numeric answer.)
questions.solution: Angles in A.P.: 2B = A + C with A + B + C = 180 deg gives 3B = 180, so B = 60 deg. Then b:c = sinB:sinC gives sqrt(3):sqrt(2) = (sqrt(3)/2):sinC, so sinC = sqrt(2)/2 and C = 45 deg (C = 135 deg impossible with B = 60). Hence A = 180 - 60 - 45 = 75 deg. (Filed: the printed answer '75 deg' belongs to this part (iii), not (ii).)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q7(iii); book p189 = PDF p216-217 (vision read); answer-label slip documented

questions.knowledgeNote: Try B = 90 deg first: sinB:sinC = 1:sin60 = 2:sqrt(3) matches instantly.
questions.question: AQ7(iv). In triangle ABC, if angle A = 30 deg and b:c = 2:sqrt(3), find angle B.
questions.solution: B + C = 150 deg and sinB:sinC = 2:sqrt(3). With B = 90 deg, C = 60 deg: sinB:sinC = 1:(sqrt(3)/2) = 2:sqrt(3). This satisfies the ratio, and monotonicity of sinB/sin(150 deg - B) on (0, 150 deg) makes it unique. So B = 90 deg. Matches the printed Answers: 90 deg.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q7(iv); book p189 = PDF p216-217 (vision read); matches key

questions.knowledgeNote: sin3B = 2sinB gives sinB*(1 - 4sin^2B) = 0: with B under 60 deg, sinB = 1/2.
questions.question: AQ7(v). If a = 2b and A = 3B, find the angles of the triangle.
questions.solution: a:b = sinA:sinB gives 2:1 = sin3B:sinB, so sin3B = 2sinB. With sin3B = 3sinB - 4sin^3B: 3sinB - 4sin^3B = 2sinB, i.e. sinB*(1 - 4sin^2B) = 0. Since B is a triangle angle with 3B < 180 deg, sinB != 0, so sin^2B = 1/4 and (B acute) sinB = 1/2: B = 30 deg. Then A = 90 deg, C = 60 deg. Matches the printed Answers: 90, 30, 60 deg.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q7(v); book p189 = PDF p216-217 (vision read); matches key
questions.answer: A = 90 deg, B = 30 deg, C = 60 deg

questions.knowledgeNote: Mirror of Ex Q8 with a, b swapped: (a+c)^2 - b^2 = 3ca factors to cosB = 1/2.
questions.question: AQ8. If 1/(a+b) + 1/(b+c) = 3/(a+b+c), show that angle B = 60 deg.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q8; book p189 = PDF p216-217 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: b + c = 2R*(sinB + sinC) = 4R*cos(A/2)*cos((B-C)/2): with A = 60 deg, cos(A/2) = a/(2R).
questions.question: AQ9(i). If in a triangle ABC, A = 60 deg, show that b + c = 2a*cos((B-C)/2).
questions.solution: b + c = 2R*(sinB + sinC) = 4R*sin((B+C)/2)*cos((B-C)/2) = 4R*cos(A/2)*cos((B-C)/2). With A = 60 deg, cos(A/2) = cos30 = sqrt(3)/2 and a = 2R*sin60 = 2R*sqrt(3)/2 = R*sqrt(3), so 4R*cos(A/2) = 4R*sqrt(3)/2 = 2*R*sqrt(3) = 2a. Hence b + c = 2a*cos((B-C)/2).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q9(i); book p189 = PDF p217 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: (a+c)^2 - b^2 = 3ca rearranges to a^2 + c^2 - b^2 = ca: read off cosB.
questions.question: AQ9(ii). In a triangle ABC, if angle B = 60 deg, prove that (a+b+c)*(a-b+c) = 3ca.
questions.solution: (a+b+c)*(a-b+c) = (a+c)^2 - b^2 = a^2 + c^2 + 2ac - b^2. With B = 60 deg, cosB = (a^2+c^2-b^2)/(2ac) = 1/2 gives a^2 + c^2 - b^2 = ac. Substituting: ac + 2ac = 3ca.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q9(ii); book p189 = PDF p217 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: a:b:c = 2:3:4 with s = 27 forces a = 12, b = 18, c = 24: Heron gives sqrt(27*15*9*3) = 27*sqrt(15).
questions.question: AQ10(i). If in any triangle a:b:c = 2:3:4 and s = 27, find the area of the triangle.
questions.solution: 2k + 3k + 4k = 2s = 54 gives k = 6: a = 12, b = 18, c = 24. Delta = sqrt[27*(27-12)*(27-18)*(27-24)] = sqrt(27*15*9*3) = sqrt(10935) = sqrt(729*15) = 27*sqrt(15) sq. units. Matches the printed Answers: 27*sqrt(15) sq. units.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q10(i); book pp189-190 = PDF p217 (vision read); matches key

questions.question: AQ10(iii). In a triangle ABC, if a = sqrt(2), b = sqrt(3) and c = sqrt(5), show that its area is (1/2)*sqrt(6) sq. units.
questions.solution: a^2 + b^2 = 2 + 3 = 5 = c^2, so the triangle is right angled at C. Delta = (1/2)*a*b = (1/2)*sqrt(2)*sqrt(3) = (1/2)*sqrt(6) sq. units.

questions.knowledgeNote: s = 21: sin(A/2) = sqrt[(s-b)(s-c)/(bc)] = sqrt(1/5); everything else follows by doubling.
questions.question: AQ11. In any triangle ABC, if a = 13 cms, b = 14 cms, c = 15 cms, find sin(A/2), cos(A/2), sinA, cosA and tan(A/2).

questions.knowledgeNote: a, b, c in A.P. means 2sinB = sinA + sinC: divide by 2cos(B/2) to get 2sin(B/2) = cos((A-C)/2), then use tan product formula.
questions.question: AQ12(i). If a, b, c are in A.P., prove that 3*tan(A/2)*tan(C/2) = 1.
questions.solution: 2b = a + c gives 2sinB = sinA + sinC, i.e. 4*sin(B/2)*cos(B/2) = 2*sin((A+C)/2)*cos((A-C)/2) = 2*cos(B/2)*cos((A-C)/2), so 2*sin(B/2) = cos((A-C)/2). Now tan(A/2)*tan(C/2) = [cos((A-C)/2) - cos((A+C)/2)]/[cos((A-C)/2) + cos((A+C)/2)]. Since cos((A+C)/2) = sin(B/2), this is [2*sin(B/2) - sin(B/2)]/[2*sin(B/2) + sin(B/2)] = sin(B/2)/[3*sin(B/2)] = 1/3. Hence 3*tan(A/2)*tan(C/2) = 1.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q12(i); book p190 = PDF p217 (vision read)

questions.question: AQ12(ii). If b, a, c are in A.P., prove that cos((B-C)/2) = 2*sin(A/2).
questions.solution: 2a = b + c gives 2sinA = sinB + sinC = 2*sin((B+C)/2)*cos((B-C)/2) = 2*cos(A/2)*cos((B-C)/2). Since 2sinA = 4*sin(A/2)*cos(A/2), dividing by 2*cos(A/2) gives 2*sin(A/2) = cos((B-C)/2).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q12(ii); book p190 = PDF p217 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: c + (b-a)*cosB = b*(cosA + cosB) = 2b*cos((A+B)/2)*cos((A-B)/2): the sine-rule ratio collapses to cot((B-A)/2).
questions.question: AQ13. If b - a = mc, prove that cot((B-A)/2) = (1 + m*cosB)/(m*sinB).
questions.solution: m = (b-a)/c. Then (1 + m*cosB)/(m*sinB) = [c + (b-a)*cosB]/[(b-a)*sinB]. Numerator: c + (b-a)*cosB = (a*cosB + b*cosA) + (b-a)*cosB (projection law) = b*(cosA + cosB) = 2b*cos((A+B)/2)*cos((A-B)/2) = 2b*sin(C/2)*cos((B-A)/2). Denominator: (b-a)*sinB = 2R*(sinB - sinA)*sinB = 2R*2*cos((A+B)/2)*sin((B-A)/2)*sinB = 4R*sin(C/2)*sin((B-A)/2)*sinB. Ratio: [2b*sin(C/2)*cos((B-A)/2)]/[4R*sin(C/2)*sin((B-A)/2)*sinB] = [2*2R*sinB*cos((B-A)/2)]/[4R*sin((B-A)/2)*sinB] = cos((B-A)/2)/sin((B-A)/2) = cot((B-A)/2).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q13; book p190 = PDF p217 (vision read)
